In a civil court, the judge is only responsible for the procedure and does not 'judge' the case. The one sitting in the main hall and asking questions is the county magistrate. A judge's actions are roughly 'What is the plaintiff's claim?' 'How does the defendant respond?' 'What is the plaintiff's evidence?' 'What is the defendant's evidence?' For a judge to ask 'If you didn't hit them, why would you help them up?' during a trial violates all the logic of a modern civil court. Anyone who has been to court knows that this is simply a joke. On July 30, 2018, I was waiting for the subject three theory test (subject four) at a certain driving school. The system was based on calling numbers. Those whose numbers were called would go to the front of the examination room to queue up. Generally, 50-100 people were called at a time, and they entered the examination room in the order of the queue. While queuing, a girl came over and asked the lady behind me what numbers were being called. Then the lady showed her the number paper in her hand. The girl said, 'Then I'll stand here,' and stood next to the lady behind me outside the queue. After seeing this, I reminded her in a low voice: 'Everyone is queuing now, just queue up.' The girl immediately flared up: 'What does it matter to you whether I queue or not? Did I affect you? What business is it of yours to tell me what to do?' After hearing this, I looked at her directly and said: 'It's none of my business, I'm just saying.' She continued to say what business it was of mine, she was afraid her number had already passed, what did it have to do with me, and so on. I stared into her eyes again and repeated: 'It's none of my business, I'm just saying!' Only then did she shut up. In fact, even if she queued, she would definitely enter the examination room within one or two minutes. Besides, even if she cut in line, if her attitude was kind, I wouldn't have minded. (It's my fault for being nosy, I shouldn't have reminded her.) I strongly condemn those who don't follow the rules and turn around and blame others. content: I support the court's verdict. The law upholds the bottom line of human nature, and the verdict in this case shows the law's will to protect people's lives and property. If everyone supports the 'full responsibility for fault' theory in the future, then the focus of punishing and preventing dangerous accidents will change to 'punishing mistakes.' This 'full responsibility for fault' punishment seems fair and strict, but it brings more insecurity to the lives and property of the people in society. If 'full responsibility for fault' is fully implemented, then in the future, when there are accidental disputes between people, the first thing they will think of is to prove that the other party is fully responsible to protect their own interests. Then the judgment is over, and the businesses will continue as they are. There will be no warning signs, and no strengthening of safety protection. Accidents have happened, and no one can change that. But strengthening safety protection and raising safety awareness can save lives. A small warning sign cannot prevent individual tourists from climbing trees, but the absence of a warning sign is definitely a lack of awareness of safety knowledge.
